extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; aspiring mathematical problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and heuristics for solving, checking, and presenting mathematical problems: using specialization, auxiliary problems, dimensional checks, symmetry, variation, incubation, and retrospective analysis to discover and validate solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish demonstrative and heuristic syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the difference between demonstrative (deductive) reasoning, which yields conclusions of the same logical nature and fully supported by premises, and heuristic (inductive/plausible) reasoning, which yields conclusions that are more vague, directional, and only partially supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic conclusions make A 'more credible' rather than proving A false/true; they have magnitude and direction but not full expression. Heuristic premises are only part of the basis (visible part) and invisible/unarticulated reasons may later overturn the conclusion. Treat heuristic conclusions as plausible but revisable; expect honest disagreements about their strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization (test special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pass from a general set of objects to a smaller set or a single object (special case) to test conjectures or guide proof attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure about a proposed theorem, test well-known special cases (e.g., equilateral, isosceles) to gain insight. Special cases can (a) verify the claim in simple instances, (b) suggest directions for proof, or (c) reveal counterexamples. Use limiting/special cases as stepping stones and for intuition; do not dismiss extreme cases as unorthodox without checking their implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refute general statements by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a purportedly general statement, exhibit an object from the stated set that does not satisfy it (a counter-example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a simple, easily testable special case first. If it fails the test, the general claim is refuted and the problem solved. If it holds, examine modifications or other special cases to find where the assertion breaks (look for extreme or limiting cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider extreme (limiting) cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine limiting or extreme examples (e.g., vertex angle → 0° or 180°, or unusual members like whales) to test claims and to strengthen or refute inductive evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme cases are often overlooked by generalizers and so are fruitful for finding counterexamples; if the statement holds even in extreme cases, the inductive evidence becomes strong because the prospect of refutation was high. Use extremes both to seek refutation and to gain confidence in a conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent and use auxiliary problems/elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve a related, typically simpler (often special) auxiliary problem and then use a supplementary remark or auxiliary element to reduce the original problem to that auxiliary problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auxiliary problems serve as stepping stones: invent an advantageous auxiliary problem and discover an appropriate supplementary remark to pass from auxiliary to original. Example: reduce two moving ships problem to the case where one ship is at rest by adding a uniform motion to the whole system. The auxiliary problem may be less ambitious yet, with the right supplement, yields the general solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialization as a method for finding counterexamples or directions
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing a general assertion, examine simple or extended special cases, vary them, and search around for extreme cases to find counterexamples or hints toward a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with random simple instances; if they comply, attempt variations or more extended special cases to derive hints. Use examination of special cases to suggest where to look for proofs or counter-examples (example under 1 in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subconscious incubation and rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow problems to incubate: after concentrated effort, take rest or a break, enabling subconscious work to progress and often produce a bright idea later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force conscious reflection beyond limits; 'take counsel of your pillow.' Leave the problem with at least some small settled point so it can return improved. Passionate desire and tension seem necessary to set subconscious work going; mere waiting without prior effort is unlikely to produce results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice interchangeable parts and treat symmetric elements similarly; exploit symmetry to simplify reasoning and to check results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a problem is symmetric, derive profit from its interchangeable parts (e.g., treat those parts in the same fashion). Avoid destroying natural symmetry wantonly, though sometimes asymmetrical treatment is compelled. Use symmetry to check results (see section 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and anchor terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise terminology for problem concepts (conditions, hypotheses, solutions, analysis/synthesis) and anchor notions in examples to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when common words have multiple senses (e.g., 'solution' meaning object satisfying condition vs. process vs. result). When parts of a condition/hypothesis are distinct, consider distinct names (e.g., 'clause') to avoid ambiguity. Warns that some historical terms are confusing and sometimes replaced by new terms ('problem to find', 'problem to prove').

rubrics_metrics.name: Test formulas by dimension (dimensional analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace quantities by their physical dimensions to check the plausibility and structure of formulas and to deduce possible forms of dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each term of a sum must have the same dimension; the dimension of a product is product of dimensions of factors. Use the test to eliminate dimensional inconsistencies and to infer relations among exponents (example: period T of pendulum depends on l and g giving T ∝ sqrt(l/g)). Limitations: this test cannot determine pure numerical constants (e.g., 2π) nor validity limits (e.g., small oscillations). It is especially important in physics and useful for checking intermediate or final results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look back (retrospective analysis) after solving
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining a solution, survey the work and final solution to analyze difficulty, decisive ideas, obstacles, alternative methods, and possible uses of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meditate on whether the solution can be seen intuitively at a glance; compare and develop other methods; invent new problems solvable by the result or method. Digesting solved problems thoroughly leads to well-ordered, ready-to-use knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by imitation, practice, and good models
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquire problem-solving skill by imitating good teachers/authors, practicing, competing with capable peers, and reading good authors until finding a natural model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the right model to imitate; enjoy and pursue what seems simple, instructive, or beautiful. Solve problems in your line to discover your preferences and strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a checklist of probing questions judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a repertoire of diagnostic questions (e.g., 'Can you check the result?', 'Did we use all the data?') to prompt useful procedures when appropriate to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intelligent problem-solver should be prepared to ask all questions on the list but only ask those prompted by careful consideration of the problem. Recognize whether the present situation is sufficiently similar to situations where a question was previously useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate, understand purpose, and desire the solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the problem fully is necessary but insufficient; concentrate intensely, desire the solution, and commit your personality to the work for greater success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack real desire, it may be better to leave the problem alone. Intense concentration is required but may be fatiguing—use variation and breaks appropriately. The intelligent reader/listener also wants both correctness and the purpose of each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers/authors should show correctness and purpose of steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting mathematics, ensure each step is not only correct but that its purpose and how it was found are made clear to readers/listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correctly presented derivation may be inaccessible if the purpose of successive steps is incomprehensible. Emphasize motives and use questions (e.g., 'Did we use all the data?') to justify steps. This helps readers derive similar arguments themselves and keeps them engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary the problem to extract useful elements and revive interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify data or viewpoint of a problem to create new associations, extract relevant elements from memory, and maintain attention when progress stalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation creates new 'contacts' and revives hope by presenting fresh aspects; it helps extract elements from memory by association. Use intelligent variation (not mindless repetition) — e.g., change parameters to known limiting cases, and foresee properties the final result must satisfy (so you can test them later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the accessible aspect (attack from right side)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success often depends on selecting the right aspect or viewpoint of the problem — attacking the 'fortress' from an accessible side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try various standpoints and view the problem from different sides until you find the fruitful angle. Variation helps reveal which side is accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use variation and limiting-case reasoning to anticipate properties and check answers
rubrics_metrics.description: By varying parameters (e.g., letting a parameter tend to a known value) anticipate how the final formula should reduce in special cases, giving properties to test the final result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for frustum volume, check that formula reduces to a^2 h when upper base = lower base, and to a^2 h/3 when upper base = 0. Prefiguring such properties helps both in construction and later checking ('CAN YOU CHECK THE RESULT?').
